weaknesses: The central camera-agnostic generalization claim is not convincingly tested on held-out real cameras. The medical experiment uses Gaussian mixtures synthesized from one HSI source; the automotive experiment trains and tests on the same HSICity camera while adding Cityscapes data; and the satellite experiment fine-tunes on the target MSI dataset. These demonstrate mixed-modality learning or transfer, but not robust inference on an unseen real sensor.

Representing each channel only by a center wavelength ignores its spectral response curve, bandwidth, radiometric calibration, and image-processing pipeline. This is especially problematic for Cityscapes RGB values, which are processed broadband measurements rather than reflectance at three precise wavelengths. The manuscript does not explain how RGB wavelengths are assigned, preventing reproduction and weakening the physical justification for cross-camera alignment.

The comparisons contain substantial architecture and initialization confounds. In the first and third experiments, CARL uses DINOv2 initialization for spectral attention and ImageNet-pretrained EVA-02 weights, while medical baselines use different U-Net, ViT, or EVA-02 backbones. Table 2 nevertheless characterizes CARL-SSL as using only 11,000 HSI samples, omitting these large external pretraining sources when contrasting it with SpectralGPT+'s one-million-image pretraining. Model capacities also are not matched.

Evidence for the proposed spectral SSL objective is insufficient. There are no spectral-only versus spatial-only SSL ablations, no comparison with ordinary I-JEPA or another SSL objective on the same architecture and data, and no non-pretrained CARL result on SegMunich. In the automotive experiment, CARL-SSL receives additional pretraining data and improves by only 1.5 mIoU; consequently, the gain cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed spectral objective. It is also unclear whether HSICity pretraining excludes its test images.

The strongest controlled architectural result is modest: CARL improves over Hyve by only 0.6 mIoU on HSICity, with heavily overlapping reported confidence intervals. The construction of those intervals, number of random seeds, and significance-testing procedure are not reported, so claims of superiority are too strong.

The stated linear scaling in spectral dimensionality is technically inaccurate: every spectral module performs self-attention over C channel tokens, which costs O(C^2); only query-to-channel cross-attention is O(KC). Training further subsamples inputs to 16 or at most 32 channels without an ablation supporting the assertion that this does not affect performance, obscuring scalability to large hyperspectral inputs.

Reproducibility is limited by the private medical data, absence of a code-release statement, and missing details such as epochs, augmentations, crop sizes, wavelength assignments, normalization, exact dataset splits, confidence-interval construction, and random seeds. Overall, the method is plausible and potentially useful, but the evidence does not adequately isolate its contribution or support the paper's broad camera-agnostic, data-efficiency, and scalability claims.

Architectural ablations also do not isolate the gains from spectral self-attention, latent cross-attention, backbone initialization, and added compute.

The evidence for broad camera agnosticism remains incomplete. The medical experiment primarily uses synthetic filters applied to the same source imagery, and the method represents bands only through nominal center wavelengths, ignoring full spectral response functions, bandwidth, radiometric calibration, noise, and other sensor effects. More direct same-task evaluation across independently acquired real cameras would better support the central claim.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the stated code-and-weights link is absent, the medical dataset is private, and important details such as downstream training lengths, batch construction across modalities, preprocessing and normalization, RGB wavelength assignments, baseline configurations, random seeds, and confidence-interval procedures are missing. The discussion of sampling 32 versus 16 hyperspectral channels is also ambiguous.
The average-rank calculation across eleven satellite datasets is not explained despite several baselines having missing entries, making this headline aggregate difficult to interpret fairly.

The appendix's feature 'variance decomposition' uses separate in-sample regressions with different numbers of predictors for organ and sensor identity; raw averaged R-squared values are therefore not directly comparable and do not establish disentanglement. The private porcine-data experiment also lacks an explicit animal-ethics or approval statement.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning medical, automotive, and satellite imagery. CARL remains stable under synthetic spectral heterogeneity and shows substantial gains on several unseen-sensor satellite datasets, notably LoveDA and WHU-OHS.

The proposed spectral feature-prediction objective is a sensible extension of joint-embedding self-supervision, and the paper provides useful pseudocode, complexity analysis, and several architectural ablations.
The presentation is generally clear, and the computational analysis appropriately acknowledges that richer spectral processing costs more than spatial-only channel-adaptive projections.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is insufficiently controlled. Medical baselines use different U-Net or ViT architectures “depending on compatibility,” while CARL benefits from DINOv2/EVA-02 initialization. Satellite baselines also differ in pretraining data, compute, patch size, and possibly evaluation implementation. No matched-backbone, matched-data, matched-budget experiment isolates the spectral encoder's contribution.

The large-scale study omits especially relevant competitors. SpectralEarth/Spectral Adapter is identified as a channel-invariant spatio-spectral approach but is not evaluated in the satellite experiments. There are also no controlled alternatives such as wavelength-conditioned set pooling, 1D spectral convolution, self-attention without learned queries, or cross-attention without spectral self-attention.

Evidence for the novel SSL component is weak. Its principal ablation compares spatial SSL against spatial-plus-spectral SSL on one validation dataset under a reduced budget, without no-pretraining, spectral-only, pixel-reconstruction, or repeated-seed controls. In automotive segmentation, CARL-SSL exceeds DOFA by only 0.5 mIoU with heavily overlapping confidence intervals; in the satellite study, CARL without the proposed SSL is not reported.

Statistical and reproducibility reporting is inadequate. Most results lack repeated-run uncertainty; the confidence-interval construction and average-rank treatment of inapplicable models are unspecified. The abstract claims public code and weights but supplies no URL, while training schedules, preprocessing, baseline tuning, and several split details are incomplete.

“Camera-agnostic” is overstated. The method requires accurate wavelength metadata and models band centers but not spectral response widths, radiometric calibration, noise, spatial resolution, or point-spread differences. The medical experiment synthesizes bands from one HSI camera rather than testing independently acquired cameras, so it does not validate robustness to many real sensor effects.

Potential pretraining/evaluation overlap is not resolved: the pretraining corpus includes the full reported BigEarthNet collection while m-bigearthnet is a downstream benchmark. The paper should document sample-level de-duplication or explicitly frame this as transductive evaluation. It also lacks an ethics/provenance statement for the private porcine data.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: learning one model across RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral sensors with different channel counts and wavelengths.

CARL is technically coherent and modular, combining wavelength encoding, spectral self-attention, learned cross-attention queries, and a conventional spatial backbone to produce fixed-dimensional representations from variable-channel inputs.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: medical imaging, autonomous driving, and eleven satellite benchmarks. Particularly compelling results include large gains on unseen LoveDA and WHU-OHS sensors, robustness under increasing synthetic sensor heterogeneity, and improved transfer for classes omitted from hyperspectral training.

The paper compares against numerous relevant camera-specific and channel-adaptive methods and provides useful architectural ablations, class-wise results, computational analysis, pseudocode, and extensive implementation details. weaknesses: The largest concern is experimental confounding. Remote-sensing baselines differ in pretraining data, initialization, architecture, and compute, while the medical comparison assigns methods either a U-Net or ViT according to compatibility. A controlled comparison using the same backbone, pretraining corpus, optimization budget, and initialization is needed to attribute gains specifically to CARL.

Evidence for the proposed spectral SSL objective is incomplete. Its main ablation only compares spatial SSL against spatial-plus-spectral SSL on one dataset, without spectral-only training, repeated runs, or equally pretrained competing adapters. In the automotive experiment, supervised CARL is below DOFA, while CARL-SSL exceeds it by only 0.5 mIoU after additional pretraining.

Statistical reporting is insufficient: the construction of the confidence intervals and number of runs are unspecified, the automotive intervals overlap substantially, and most satellite and ablation results have no uncertainty. The average-rank calculation is also unclear for baselines that cannot run on several datasets.

The camera-agnostic claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence. The medical sensor shifts remain synthetic—even when measured filters are used—and the main evaluation stays on the original HSI sensor. CARL represents each band only by a center wavelength, omitting full spectral response and bandwidth; wavelength assignments for ordinary RGB data are not documented.

The core machinery largely combines established Fourier features, self-attention, Perceiver-style learned queries, VICReg, and I-JEPA. Comparisons against simpler common-grid spectral interpolation, DeepSets/Perceiver pooling, and ablations separating spectral self-attention from cross-attention would better establish novelty and necessity.

Reproducibility remains limited because the code-and-weights URL is blank, the porcine dataset is private, several downstream training details and split procedures are missing, and ethical approval or provenance for the animal data is not stated.
